newsitem.title: ITALY: Separatist commandos seize Venice belltower.
newsitem.headline: Separatist commandos seize Venice belltower.

text.p: Italian separatists, believed to be armed, smashed their way into the belltower in St Mark's Square in Venice on Friday and occupied it to demand an independent northern state, police said.

State radio said around 10 men in military-style fatigues staged the dramatic raid, using what appeared to be a six-wheeled armoured vehicle to crash through the entrance to the 99-metre (325-foot) tower by the Grand Canal.
"They are armed with (light) machine guns. It is a proper military operation," the radio's correspondent reported from the lagoon city.
The group unfurled a banner of the former Venetian republic at the top of the monument, one of the world's most famous landmarks.
About 300 police were in the square and two police helicopters hovered overhead, reporters at the scene said.
Police headquarters in Venice gave no further details.

Italian media said the group had forced the captain of a ferry they had boarded shortly after midnight to dock by the square, where they had driven their vehicle off and headed for the base of the belltower.
Police had tried to talk to the group but one of its members had replied that they were waiting to speak "to our ambassador". It was not clear what they meant.
Italian television news broadcasts in northeast Italy have been regularly interrupted over the past few months by a mystery group calling for the restoration of a Venetian state.

The pirate broadcasts have spoken of a "spectacular action" in the canal city on May 12, the 200th anniversary of the demise of the centuries-old "Most Serene Republic" of Venice at the hands of Napoleonic forces.

"We knew something might happen around the anniversary of the fall of the Venice republic but no one could have imagined it would come to this," local councillor Mara Rumiz was quoted by the news agency ANSA as saying.

Separatist sentiment has grown in affluent northern Italy in the 1990s, spurred first by political corruption scandals and later by growing resentment at high taxation and stifling central bureaucacy.

The main secessionist party, the Northern League, last September symbolically declared a separate northern republic of "Padania" at a rally in Venice but has denied it is behind the recent spate of pirate television broadcasts.
The northeast Veneto region around Venice, one of Italy's richest areas, is not one of the League's primary powerbases.
The League was badly bloodied in a first round of voting in local elections on April 27, losing power in a host of cities and provinces including Milan, Italy's financial capital.

Party leader Umberto Bossi this week urged his followers not to vote for the "Rome" parties in the runoff second round of voting to be held on Sunday. "We'll send everybody off to the mountains," he said.
Many people in the wealthy north begrudge the large sums of state aid given to the impoverished south of Italy, suspecting much ends up in the hands of organised crime.
